summary: Funk: 95-115 BPM, a dry live kit locked on the one with ghost notes, a syncopated bass that leads, one- or two-chord dominant 9th vamps stabbed on clavinet like a rhythm guitar, short horn stabs; knowledge/style/funk.json is its template
body: Tempo 95-115 BPM (90-110 for the slow, heavy grooves; around 100 is typical), straight 16ths.

Drums: a live kit, tuned high and kept dry (little or no reverb on kick, snare or hats); 8th or 16th hats, ghost notes on the snare, the kick locking with the bass; everything lands hard on the one; few fills.
Bass: the centrepiece: a syncopated finger or slap line with octaves, 16th ghost notes and slides into the one, leaving space after it; it plays against the kick and leads the groove.

Harmony: one chord for a long time or a two-chord vamp: dominant 7ths and 9ths (E9, E7#9), or i7-IV7 dorian; on clavinet played like a rhythm guitar (short, sharp, percussive 16th figures), Rhodes in sparse three-note voicings, organ; short stabs, never held pads.
Lead: horns (trumpets and saxes) in unison stabs of an 8th or less, often anticipating the beat; a short repeated vocal or synth phrase.
Texture/master: dry, warm, analog and live; bass and drums up front; space between the parts, nothing washed in reverb.

Sources (2026-11-26): MusicRadar 'How to funk-up your keyboard parts in 5 easy steps' and 'David Garibaldi: 12 tips for funk drumming'; Splice 'Genre focus series: funk'; UJAM 'How to use slap bass like 90s funk legends'; Keyboard Magazine 'Funk up your keyboard parts'.
Apply: pattern/gmd-funk-beat-1 on the drums, then pattern/dorian-i-IV on the keys four bars later. For a whole style change the Team Lead's restyle uses knowledge/style/funk.json instead.

drums.about: the drum track (a kit); leave out if there isn't one

keys.about: a chordal part (keys, pad); leave out if there isn't one

key.about: the project's key; leave out to estimate it from the notes
